title: Certify each AI tool for its use case, approve centrally, recertify
problem: Quality-management processes were built for transparent, deterministic tools, making it hard to decide how much testing AI needs before deployment and how to monitor it.
approach: The FRC treats a tool in its use case as the unit of certification, testing inputs, logic and outputs.
Deloitte UK's Technology Controls Board, set up in April 2026, reviews tools before pilot and deployment (self-reported).
FRC found recertification typically formal only on change; two firms had owners confirm annually, one enforced a three-year backstop (independent).
Tool owner, methodology and business approve certification; quality leadership decides whether to recertify after a trigger.

title: Risk-tiered permitted-use policy with approved tools, barred uses and a prompt library
problem: Staff will use general AI tools unless the firm says which are allowed, and most large UK firms applied one certification process regardless of risk.
approach: The firm lists permitted tools and uses, bars some uses and scales validation to risk; PwC US began with pre-approved administrative work.
Deloitte UK describes use-case governance with risk thresholding, triage and a clearing house; no result is published (self-reported).
PCAOB staff found some firms barred GenAI in audit procedures while others allowed it for administrative tasks and initial drafts.
The engagement partner is responsible for appropriate use of approved tools.
who: PwC US, Deloitte UK, FRC, PCAOB staff

title: Authorised-tool inventory and preventive controls against unapproved or outdated AI tools
problem: AI tools multiply faster than firms approve them, and the FRC found firms generally did not monitor that teams used only authorised, current tools.
approach: Firms keep inventories of current certified tools and versions and use preventive controls such as authorised repositories and blocked installs.
Most of six large UK firms kept such inventories (independent); over a third of professionals admit using unauthorised AI (vendor-published).
Unapproved or outdated tools found in use are escalated; exceptions are approved by a named function.
who: FRC, IFIAR, six large UK firms

title: Test sets and parallel running before and during limited AI rollout
problem: No public benchmark or firm result says how often an audit agent's output is wrong in live use, and tolerance for deficient output is a judgement.
approach: Firms build representative test sets and score tool output before release and after model changes; IFIAR lists benchmarking against traditional methods.
The FRC says firms may release a tool to a few teams first, which often run alternative procedures in parallel.
An independent benchmark found frontier models complete much staff-level audit work but sometimes write incorrect documentation; no parallel-run results are published.

title: Embed methodology in AI-tool design and validate assurance from AI procedures
problem: A firm's methodology may permit approaches that fail auditing standards even when the tool works, and IFIAR's top technology findings were misreading tool results and thin testing of outliers.
approach: Methodology teams join tool development, and certification validates the supporting methodology against auditing standards.
In the FRC's contract-review example, assurance from the AI procedure depends on confidence in the tool's risk indicators and sampling.
IFIAR members reporting a tool not used as intended: 31% in 2024, 29% in 2023 (independent).
Engagement teams test data inputs and a sample of low-risk-rated items.

title: Due diligence and revalidation for third-party AI tools, scaled for small firms
problem: Firms usually take the foundation model from a third party and cannot evaluate its training data, and smaller firms lack the specialists the FRC guidance assumes.
approach: All six largest UK firms considered vendor controls, data security and confidentiality; the FRC says firms may rely on independent assurance.
NFRA calls for contract terms on data protection, explainability documentation and audit rights; CPAB points to SOC 2 reports for off-the-shelf tools.
Grant Thornton UK advised smaller firms to start with granular, easily checked tasks.
Procurement, security and methodology approve the vendor; the firm re-approves when the model changes.
who: FRC, CPAB, NFRA, Grant Thornton UK

title: Monitor AI tool use and audit-quality impact; settle who monitors network tools
problem: Firms count tool usage, mostly for licensing, but do not quantify effect on audit quality, and it is sometimes unclear who monitors a globally built tool.
approach: IFIAR describes thematic reviews with metrics such as false-positive and false-negative rates against a manual sample, rework rates and usage dashboards.
FRC found none of the six largest UK firms quantified audit-quality impact (independent); the AFM found usage mostly estimated, not measured.
Quality leadership reviews tool-impact metrics and decides to restrict, retrain or recertify.

title: Board oversight of AI in the quality plan, with an AI committee
problem: Using AI reaches into governance, resources, acceptance, ethics and engagement performance, and unexpected AI failures may not reach the tool owner or quality function.
approach: Deloitte UK's independent Audit Governance Board reviewed its Single Quality Plan, now covering AI, with a human in the loop central.
IFIAR suggests formal escalation paths, user feedback on fitness, AI oversight committees and whistleblowing procedures covering AI use.
No outcome is published (self-reported).
The committee or tool owner decides to pause, restrict or re-approve a tool after an incident.

title: ISO/IEC 42001 certification of the firm's own AI management system
problem: Firms need external reference points for governing their own AI use, and SEC staff said there is no single authority or framework for AI governance.
approach: KPMG announced in November 2025 it achieved ISO 42001 certification, which it described as independent validation of its internal AI management systems.
KPMG said it is the first Big Four firm to achieve it, and called it a precursor to providing AI assurance services.
The announcement does not say which KPMG entity was certified; no quality measurement is published (self-reported).

title: Role-based AI training tied to tool access, with in-workflow micro-training
problem: Reviewers who cannot judge when AI output is wrong cannot review it, and untrained staff was the top-ranked blocker to audit transformation in a 54-firm survey.
approach: Training is differentiated by user group and covers automation bias and known tool weaknesses; tool access is conditional on completed training.
PwC made GenAI training mandatory before ChatPwC access, per an academic reading; KPMG trained all auditors in prompt engineering.
Deloitte announced on 24 June 2026 a tutor mode in Omnia giving on-demand micro-training, without evidence of use (self-reported).

title: Connected engagement resourcing in one tool, with the AI role unspecified
problem: ISQM 1 requires firms to assign personnel with the competence and capacity for engagements, and RSM describes replacing manual staffing and budgeting processes.
approach: RSM describes Luca Resourcing as a connected tool for staffing requests, budget planning and engagement-leader review.
The post lists it among RSM's AI-related investments but does not say what AI does inside it.
No outcome is published; RSM says it improves visibility into engagement planning (self-reported).
The engagement leader reviews and approves the staffing plan and budget.

title: Firm-approved guidance assistant for audit research, grounded in the firm's own manuals
problem: Auditors spend time finding and applying the firm's own manuals and practice aids, and generic chatbots can produce hallucinations, omissions and distortions.
approach: RSM US launched Ask Luca on 8 January 2026, giving guidance from its manuals and practice aids to 4,000+ assurance professionals (self-reported).
Deloitte UK launched a Research Assistant chatbot; Plante Moran piloted CoCounsel with 140+ participants, 91% saying it was faster (vendor-published).
The auditor checks the source guidance and applies own judgement; complex questions still go to technical consultation.
who: RSM US, Deloitte UK, Plante Moran

title: Engage regulators early on new AI tools and keep an inspection-ready file
problem: Standards do not yet address AI directly, regulators say they will inspect AI use, and no AICPA peer-review guidance on AI tools was found.
approach: The FRC's AI Sandbox, opened 4 June 2026, gives selected UK firms about three meetings with FRC experts; participants are not named.
PCAOB inspectors meet firms to understand AI use, and many firms invited inspectors to pilot demonstrations.
A small firm could assemble a list of AI tools, approvers and review steps before peer review (an idea).
Quality leadership decides what to bring to regulators; tool owners answer inspector questions from the central file.

title: AI in a firm's own quality monitoring and remediation (vendor tool announced)
problem: Inspectors find firms' own monitoring weak; IFIAR counted 21 findings in 2025 for failing to identify audit performance issues in internal inspections.
approach: AuditFile announced QualityLink on 4 Dec 2025, which it says uses agentic AI to flag firm-level quality risks and track corrective actions.
The release names no customer and gives no figures (vendor-published); the SEC asks auditors how they use AI to monitor quality.
Quality leadership decides which root causes are real; remediation owners sign off actions.

title: Idea: independent third-party validation of audit firms' own AI tools
problem: Idea, not a deployment: smaller firms without in-house expertise may want someone to confirm an AI tool works as intended.
approach: Idea discussed on an ICAEW podcast: Deloitte's Martin Brown said third-party providers should test and evaluate tools for the use case.
Grant Thornton UK's Jon Morris said smaller firms would take more comfort from a provider partnering with a large firm.
The firm decides what weight to give third-party validation when approving a tool.

title: Firm-wide audit programmes on an AI-enabled platform, updated centrally after inspection findings
problem: Sanville & Company, a 20-person firm, found its legacy platform limited its methodology, with sample-heavy testing creating bottlenecks as a new quality-control standard approached.
approach: Sanville built audit programmes in Fieldguide; after a PCAOB exam flagged an issue, it pushed the updated programme to every open engagement.
First PCAOB inspection run entirely on the platform had zero comment forms (vendor-published).
Caseware announced Citrin Cooperman and PKF O'Connor Davies implemented its audit suite; no review result is published.
Partners update programmes and reviewers approve work on the platform.

title: Idea: engagement leader plans AI use upfront; senior team reviews it
problem: Idea, not a deployment: ISA 220 makes the partner responsible for review, but hard-to-explain tool outputs complicate direction, supervision and review.
approach: Idea in guidance: IFIAR asks engagement leaders to set expectations at the outset for planned AI uses on the engagement.
Senior team members reflect at the end on overall technology use and whether scepticism was maintained.
The AICPA practice aid says partners must understand the tools and ensure the firm approved them.

title: Human control points built into agentic audit workflows, with escalation and approval
problem: Agents run multi-step procedures, so there is no single output to review, and without defined review points errors compound.
approach: The FRC separates review of final outputs from oversight at control points and lets a tool escalate when uncertain.
Deloitte UK says teams critically assess and approve agent results before use; KPMG says Clara agents work in concert with human review.
Neither reports review results; the control is design intent (self-reported).
A competent team member authorises the agent to continue and approves preliminary conclusions.

title: Review mechanics for AI output: citations, traces, source tie-back, confirmation gates
problem: A confident, well-formatted AI output can pass review with less challenge than a junior's work, and output without sources cannot be checked efficiently.
approach: The FRC's examples have the tool cite stable document identifiers for every extract; CPAB's example compares extracted data to the contract.
The AFM saw workflows where a step completes only after the auditor confirms the output is supported by evidence.
PwC, Fieldguide, RSM and Andera describe evidence trails or run traces; no detection or override rate is published.
who: FRC, AFM, PwC, Fieldguide, RSM, Andera

title: Idea: structured scepticism, forming an independent view before checking the AI answer
problem: Idea, not a deployment: in an experiment, auditors relying on automated tools were less sceptical than when relying on a team member.
approach: Idea in guidance: the FRC says reviewers may form an independent view first, such as reading source material before an AI summary.
In the Peters experiment a counter-arguing mindset reduced the loss of scepticism; the AFM saw auditors assess fraud risk themselves first.
The reviewer records an independent view before opening the AI output; a supervisor spot-checks the challenge.

title: AI review of engagement files for omissions and inconsistencies before reviewer sign-off
problem: Reviewers spend time on completeness and consistency checks that take attention from judgemental areas, and review is a bottleneck.
approach: Deloitte UK reports Smart Review was fully deployed in the year to 31 May 2025; all FTSE audits have access (self-reported).
KPMG says Clara agents can review engagement documentation; PIA Group's CIO describes AI running hundreds of checks on one file (self-reported).
Neither firm describes how reviewers use the output; the reviewer resolves every AI-raised exception.

title: Idea: second model or rules-based check on AI output, then human
problem: Idea, not a deployment: generative tools are probabilistic, and human reviewers cannot catch every deficiency in high-volume AI output.
approach: Idea in regulator guidance: the FRC lists one LLM reviewing another, several LLMs with a selector, and rules-based checks.
The AICPA practice aid, as reported, says a second tool does not reduce the auditor's supervision and review responsibility.
A human takes over when components disagree or the checker is unsure.

title: Document AI use in a central tool record and the engagement file
problem: Inspectors cannot challenge AI-assisted work if the file does not show where AI was used and how the team responded.
approach: The FRC's June 2025 guidance keeps certification centrally; the audit file holds tool version, prompts, fitness assessment and how outputs informed conclusions.
IFIAR asks firms to explain how auditor judgement was applied to AI outputs.
FRC found firms with engagement-specific tools required templates on file, though some wording made completion look optional (independent).

title: Disclose AI use to clients and audit committees through engagement letters
problem: Clients worry about where their data goes and whether it trains models, and a Grant Thornton UK director said a few would not sign up.
approach: Grant Thornton UK uses clear engagement-letter terms on AI use and in some cases ring-fences work from model training.
Deloitte's Martin Brown said very few clients had asked the firm not to use GenAI.
A Foley article suggests audit committees ask what the auditor does with AI; the engagement leader agrees AI-use terms with the client.

title: Redesign supervision and early-career development as juniors review AI output
problem: If tools do the first-pass work juniors used to do, juniors lose the practice that built judgement while firms lean on them to review tool output.
approach: PwC's AI assurance leader said in August 2025 that new hires would function like managers in three years, overseeing AI.
PwC said assurance training is moving back to basics, with earlier time on critical thinking and professional scepticism.
IFIAR asks firms to prioritise supervision training; no outcome is published (self-reported).

title: Idea: put AI tools in the SQMS 1 risk assessment and evaluation
problem: Idea, not a deployment: US firms must first evaluate their quality-management system by 15 Dec 2026, and public starting material shows no AI line.
approach: Idea from standard-setter guidance: the AICPA practice aid, 13 Oct 2026, says audit firms should set quality-management policies for AI tools.
A small firm would add AI as quality risks and responses in its existing risk assessment and annual evaluation.
No firm reports having done this.

title: Govern firm-built and staff-built agents through a governed platform or review gates
problem: Staff can build their own automations and agents with AI tools, creating unreviewed software and agent access to client data.
approach: Caseware launched an Agentic Pioneer Program on 4 Jun 2026; PKF O'Connor Davies joined 8 Oct 2026 and will get priority access.
No agent in use is described; SAV Associates' founding partner published a 75-point security checklist with review, change management and least-privilege access.
Higher-risk agent actions need human approval; agents have named owners and review before entering workflows.
who: Caseware, PKF O'Connor Davies, SAV Associates

title: Outside capital funds firm-wide AI investment while attest stays CPA-owned
problem: Accounting firms are often capital-constrained because most profits go to partners, restricting investment in technology and acquisitions.
approach: CFO Brew reported Crowe agreed a majority sale to KKR and Eide Bailly to Reverence Capital; both wanted more capital for AI.
Both firms are to adopt alternative practice structures separating attest from other lines; no AI programme funded by the deals is published.
Oath describes itself as an AI-native audit firm with a financial proof platform; no Oath client or result is published.
